questions.q: What is Chapter 5's job, relative to the design decisions made in Chapters 2 through 4?
options: To formalize already-made decisions into the actual artifacts a real engagement hands to a client, not to redesign anything
To introduce entirely new design decisions not covered earlier
To replace Chapters 2 through 4's decisions with simpler alternatives
To repeat Chapter 1's requirements gathering in more detail
questions.explain: Chapter 5 turns already-made decisions into formal deliverables; if a new design decision needs to be made while writing a deliverable, that signals something was left unresolved earlier, not that Chapter 5 should resolve it.

questions.q: Why should Service Contract's connection to Equipment Asset be drawn with master-detail notation specifically, rather than a plain line, in the ERD?
options: Because plain lines are not supported by any diagramming tool
Because master-detail relationships cannot be diagrammed at all
Because the relationship type itself is architecturally meaningful, and a reviewer should be able to see it from the diagram alone without needing prose to explain it
Because Equipment Asset only has one relationship in the entire data model
questions.explain: The diagram notation itself should carry the information that this is master-detail (not lookup), since Lesson 9 chose that relationship type deliberately and the diagram should communicate that choice visibly.

questions.q: What does a data dictionary add that the ERD alone does not provide?
options: A list of every stakeholder involved in the project
Field-level detail for each object, such as Equipment Asset's indexed Serial_Number__c external ID
The company's full risk register
A replacement for the ERD that makes diagrams unnecessary
questions.explain: The data dictionary carries field-level specifics (types, purposes, key fields like Serial_Number__c) that would make the diagram unreadable if crammed in — the two are companion artifacts, not substitutes for each other.

questions.q: What does this lesson say should NOT be crammed directly onto the data model diagram?
options: The objects and relationships themselves
The names of the entities in the model
The master-detail versus lookup distinction
Every field, validation rule, and automation detail, which belongs in the dictionary or technical architecture document instead
questions.explain: Field-level detail, validation rules, and automation logic belong in supporting prose or the data dictionary; cramming them into the diagram turns it into an unreadable wall of boxes that defeats its purpose.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the data model diagram is usually the first artifact an Architecture Review Board examines?
options: Because it's the fastest way to sanity-check whether the rest of the design holds together — if the data model doesn't make sense, nothing built on top of it can be trusted either
Because it is the shortest document to read
Because ARBs are only ever interested in data, never in security or integration
Because the diagram replaces the need for a technical architecture document
questions.explain: A board checks the data model first because every other design area (security, integration, the portal) is built on top of it — if the foundation doesn't hold together, nothing built on it can be trusted.
